deep.reconstruction: This page contains no mathematics. It is a page of German lecture notes or excerpts on ancient Greek history, continuing from folio 77 (Themistocles and Aristides) and running into folio 79 (Thermopylae, Artemisium, Salamis, Plataea, Mycale). The hand and the subject suggest notes from a history course, not a working sheet of Gauss's. Content in order: (1) Themistocles' view that battles like Marathon could not always be fought again, but that the Persians could be resisted with a navy. (2) The Athenians were persuaded to build a fleet of 100 warships from the revenues of the (Laurion) silver mines, which made Athens a naval power and the mightiest state. (3) The new Persian invasion of 480 BC; Themistocles is called the saviour of Greece. (4) His failed attempt to unite all Greeks, because of the many small states and Persian sympathisers such as the Boeotians. (5) Sparta demanded the supreme command and Themistocles gave way. (6) A congress first decided to hold the Vale of Tempe, then chose Thermopylae, which was entrusted to the Spartans under Leonidas. (7) The fleet was the main matter: the Athenians could not hold their city, and Themistocles persuaded them to abandon it and take to the ships. (8) Meanwhile Xerxes advanced across the Hellespont through Thrace and Macedonia. There are no derivations, formulas or computations to reconstruct.
errors: No mathematical content, so there are no mathematical errors.

Historical detail: Herodotus (7.144) gives 200 ships for Themistocles' naval programme of c. 483/482 BC. Plutarch and Aristotle's Athenaion Politeia give 100. The figure of 100 is therefore one tradition, not an error.
The deleted number before the correction '480' looks in the image more like '408' (a slip) than '100'. The corrected date of 480 BC for Xerxes' invasion is right.

results.what: Narrative notes on Themistocles' naval policy and the opening of Xerxes' invasion of 480 BC (Tempe, Thermopylae, evacuation of Athens)
results.usually_credited_to: Herodotus and Plutarch (ancient sources), as presented in standard early-19th-century history lectures
